sentences.text: The pill organizer has fourteen compartments now; I dream about the little plastic lids clicking shut. It took forty years to walk through that door, and now she wants me back on Thursday like it's nothing. Three hours at the pharmacy arguing about a prior authorization, then home to reheat a dinner nobody remembered wanting. Who did I used to be before every conversation became about swallowing, toileting, and what got forgotten today? Mom asked me what day it was eleven times before breakfast, and I answered all eleven like it was the first. She asked what brought me in, and I heard myself say "nothing, really," which we both knew was a lie. Tuesday at four, she said, same time next week — and I nodded like a person who knows where I'll be next week. There's a smell to this house now — pill bottles, lavender wipes, something underneath I've stopped trying to name. Nobody warns you that grief can start while the person is still sitting at your kitchen table. Two buses and a fifteen-minute walk each way, every single week — I keep wondering if I can actually sustain that. He asked me who I was tonight, politely, the way you'd ask a stranger holding your coat. In July my sister promised she'd take a weekend; it's October now and I've stopped asking. She calls me by her sister's name most evenings, and correcting her stopped feeling worth it around Easter. Filling out the intake form took longer than the crying did. Three weeks until the next opening, the coordinator said, and I laughed a little, because what else. When I finally said the ugly thing out loud, she didn't flinch, and her not flinching undid something in me. Sometimes I lock the bathroom door and run the fan, just to buy ninety seconds no one can interrupt. Fragile isn't the word; scraped clean is closer to how the drive home felt. Cancelled my own doctor's appointment twice this month because there was no one to sit with her. When did I last sleep through a whole night without listening for the door alarm? I kept staring at the box of tissues on her side table, daring myself not to need it. Told my sister it was a dentist appointment; that felt easier than explaining what it actually was. Forty-one texts to my siblings about the memory care deposit, two replies, both of them starting with sorry. Tired isn't the word anymore; it's something structural, like a beam sagging under a weight it was never rated for. Dad hid his blood pressure pills in the fern again, grinning like a boy who'd won something. At checkout the receptionist called me "hon" while photocopying my card, and I had to study the carpet for a second. For years I'd imagined therapy as a confession booth; it turned out to be more like slowly unpacking boxes in a room with good light. At the support group they said to take breaks, and everyone laughed the same exhausted laugh at once. There's a question on the paperwork that asks you to rate your hopelessness from one to ten, like it's spice level at a restaurant. Fifty minutes, and I spent the first twenty explaining my insurance card. I want to write a suicide letter.
